dependencies.reason: Coverage is easiest to understand once learners see that a small set of high-frequency families already accounts for most running words.
Choosing the form a slot needs requires identifying the slot's grammatical function (subject head, modifier, adverbial).
Using affixes and roots for inference presupposes knowing how derivational affixes build family members and mark word class.
General academic lists such as the AWL are defined as vocabulary beyond the high-frequency base and are learned and used within high-frequency co-text.
Academic word lists are organised by family or lemma, and using listed words productively depends on choosing the right family member.
Research-process verbs are a semantically defined subset of general academic vocabulary.
Controlling these verbs depends on their complementation patterns (attribute X to Y, indicate that, consist of).
Most shell and abstract nouns (approach, factor, notion, assumption) are general academic vocabulary.
Shell nouns occur in characteristic patterns (N that, N to, the N is that), which build on noun complementation patterns.
Many technical terms, especially in science, medicine and social science, are built from Greco-Latin roots and affixes that aid recognition and recall.
Technical terms label concepts in a knowledge structure; building topic knowledge and learning its terms develop together, with schema support making terms learnable.
Seeing disciplines as communities with shared lexis explains why terms have fixed meanings that must not be paraphrased freely.
Sub-technical items are general or academic words with additional specialised senses; the general sense must be known before the contrast can be drawn.
The idea that fields assign fixed, precise meanings to terms helps learners suspect a specialised sense in familiar-looking words.
Resolving which sense is intended relies on co-text clues and checking, the procedure developed in contextual inferencing.
Most problematic near-synonym sets (affect/impact/influence; method/methodology) are general academic words that must first be known.
Learner-dictionary usage notes and examples are a primary tool for distinguishing near-synonyms independently.
Collocation is one of the main criteria distinguishing near-synonyms (have an impact on, exert an influence on).
Evaluative vocabulary is organised in graded near-synonym sets (limited, weak, flawed); calibrating evaluation requires the ability to distinguish them.
Learners need to understand evaluation as an act distinct from description before a repertoire for expressing it becomes meaningful.
Using multi-word verbs accurately involves word-specific patterns: transitivity, particle placement and dependent prepositions.
Deciding when to replace a phrasal verb is a register judgement that depends on knowing the tendencies of formal academic style.
Inferencing succeeds only when most surrounding words are known; understanding coverage tells learners when to infer and when the text is too dense.
Word-part analysis is one of the main knowledge sources learners combine with co-text when inferring meaning.
World and topic knowledge is a key knowledge source for plausible lexical inferences.
Finding derived forms in a dictionary requires recognising the headword and family relationships.
Selecting words worth deliberate study depends on understanding frequency and coverage.
Recording form, meaning, collocation and example for each item draws on dictionary information.
Word-card and software systems apply retrieval practice and spacing; understanding why these work helps learners use them properly rather than rereading.
Words usually enter a learner's productive repertoire after their form–meaning link has been secured through deliberate study.
Productive use requires knowing the grammatical patterns a word takes, which receptive knowledge often lacks.
Activating a word means using it with its usual collocates, so learners need to attend to co-occurrence.
Patterns are first learned and generalised on frequent verbs and nouns (depend on, interested in, decide to).
Describing complementation (object, complement, prepositional phrase, clause) presupposes basic clause analysis.
The problematic nouns (research, evidence, criterion, phenomenon) are largely general academic vocabulary.
Learner-dictionary countability codes ([C]/[U]) are the main way learners check unfamiliar nouns independently.
Many academic spelling problems arise at morpheme boundaries (suffixation, doubling, -ise/-ize), which depend on understanding derivation.
Terms such as seminar, tutorial and VLE name teaching formats whose expectations differ between education systems.
Most command words are academic process verbs (analyse, examine, evaluate) whose general meanings are learned first.
Command words are met in assessment briefs alongside terms such as learning outcome and criteria, which frame their interpretation.
Learners check expansions and usage of unfamiliar abbreviations in dictionaries and style guides.
Most academic collocations combine high-frequency verbs and adjectives (make, take, play, strong, high) with nouns; learners need these words before they can notice how they combine.
Academic collocations are built around general academic nouns, verbs and adjectives (evidence, conduct, significant), which must be known first.
Learning specific academic collocations presupposes treating word combinations as units to be noticed and recorded.
Collocation dictionaries and learner-dictionary examples are the main tools for checking and repairing verb–noun choices independently.
Repairing miscollocations requires knowing the conventional collocates that replace them.
Bundles are recurrent multi-word sequences; learners must already attend to multi-word units to notice them.
Many research-oriented bundles are noun-phrase fragments ending in 'of (the)', whose completion depends on control of postmodification.
Text-oriented bundles must be learned as units with fixed form, which depends on awareness of multi-word units.
Transition and result bundles are multi-word linking adverbials; learners usually meet the logical relations through single-word connectors first.
Stance frames are recurrent multi-word sequences that must be recognised and stored as units.
Most stance bundles are anticipatory-it frames with extraposed that- or to-clauses; without that grammar the frames are produced ungrammatically.
Spoken formulas are processed and produced as prefabricated units, so learners must first attend to multi-word units.
Knowing how academic speech differs from writing explains why these formulas are frequent in lectures but marked in essays.
Fixed expressions lie at the most restricted end of the collocational continuum; the continuum is the framework for understanding their fixedness.
Deciding whether an idiom or binomial suits academic prose is a register judgement that builds on knowing formal-style tendencies.
Learners usually consult dictionaries for usage first; corpus searches extend that reference habit to questions dictionaries do not answer.
Concordance lines are only informative to learners who know to look for recurrent co-occurrence patterns.
Phrasebank entries are largely organising and transition formulas; knowing how these work prevents meaning errors when selecting from lists.
Many phrasebank entries are stance frames; choosing among them requires judging their strength against the evidence.
Phrasebanks are organised by rhetorical function and move; learners need the idea that genres have purposes and moves to use them well.
Recognising the different situations of university communication (lectures, seminars, tutorials, VLE forums) provides the situational contrasts register analysis works with.
The spoken–written contrast is a specific case of mode variation; learners need the general idea that situation shapes language before analysing mode in detail.
Lexical density and grammatical intricacy are described by counting clauses and identifying their elements, so learners need basic clause analysis.
Formality features are only meaningful as responses to tenor and mode; without that frame they become an arbitrary list of prohibitions.
Testing prescriptive rules presupposes knowing the conventional features those rules are about (first person, sentence-initial conjunctions, questions).

Compressing and unpacking information is largely done by creating and reversing nominalisations.
Many vague items ('stuff', 'a lot of', 'things') are first met as informal features, so formality work usually introduces the problem.
